name: Colin Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not tied to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and this interview is confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew that finds faults and joints power cables under busy streets. I have a two-year technical diploma, but no classroom picture prepares you for a pit filling with rainwater. A clean joint that lasts is still the part I love.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What takes the most energy outside the repair itself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Permits, traffic and explaining to shop owners why the trench cannot close yet. I use an AI assistant every day to draft job packs, then check the routes and cable numbers myself. On Thursdays I teach a paid evening cable class at the technical college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I would say the software is still useful for drafting a permit list, even if the bigger promises fade. The street does not open itself and a cable joint still needs two steady hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Mariam has a nursing wage, and we have a few months of expenses saved. I could keep doing the cable work until the retirement date we are discussing, though I would be disappointed that the technology did not go further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the underground crew as I do now and keep checking the AI job pack against the survey. I would still teach cable jointing on Thursday evenings at the technical college; it is paid work I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little professional disappointment. The bills do not look different in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake does the job pack make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sometimes puts a delivery beside the wrong street entrance. I catch it on the plan before a truck blocks the shop next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more on new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The assistant I already use is enough for permit lists, and I would rather spend the equipment money on tested cable gear.

say: I would tell the depot the **AI job pack** remains useful for permits despite modest wider results.
I would remind the crew that **cable joints** still need skilled hands beneath the street.
think: Mariam’s **nursing wage** and our few months saved make our current retirement discussion plausible.
I would be **disappointed** that the technology stayed narrow, while my own pay looks stable.
do: Keep **underground crew work** and check existing AI job packs against surveys.
Continue the paid **Thursday cable class** at the technical college.
feel: **Calm**, with mild disappointment about what the technology failed to do.
S0.quote: The street does not open itself and a cable joint still needs two steady hands.
fieldNote: He already uses AI daily, so continued job-pack checking is **routine work**.
His wife’s wage and moderate savings support a **calm outlook**, and the evening class is existing income.

steps.text: Keep leading underground cable repairs and checking existing job packs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say automated permits might save hours, but the crews and shop owners must see the route before a street closes. I would bring that issue to our union safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could cut permit clerks and push more paperwork onto my team. I think my hands-on job remains, though losing a paid evening class if the college cuts costs would reduce our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the next union safety meeting and ask for a crew review of AI permit routes. I would also learn the new AI permit system when the company introduces it, then test one job on Market Street against the old records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office change and anxious if my teaching income ends. The underground crew itself still has a lot of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A map showing where a machine-suggested road closure would block the clinic entrance. I want a named reviewer before the permit goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does teaching matter at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It covers some of our daughter’s study costs. If the college cancels my class, Mariam and I would have to redraw that support, even with her wage.

say: I would seek a **crew review** of AI permit routes before any street closure.
I would raise **clinic access** and shop deliveries at the union safety meeting.
think: My **field job** probably survives, but the paid college class could disappear if the school cuts costs.
Losing **teaching income** would change how Mariam and I help our daughter study.
do: Join the next **union safety meeting** with a map of the clinic access risk.
Learn the new **AI permit system** when introduced and test a Market Street job.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic household income loss despite a secure cable crew role.
S1.quote: I want a named reviewer before the permit goes out.
fieldNote: He separates his robust **field role** from a vulnerable paid evening class.
His union proposal names a **specific safety check**, while new permit-system learning is beyond his existing AI use.

steps.text: Join the union safety meeting with a clinic access map
Learn the new AI permit system and test a Market Street job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 can clear permits but cannot make a safe joint underground. Around 2031 a capable robot might, and I want a human testing the first one beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I planned to work about five more years if our accounts allow it, so 2031 is uncomfortably close to my exit. The company might cut crew numbers before I stop, and the college class could go sooner if the college buys automated lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union branch to press for paid field trials with a human sign-off. If the company offers a paid cable-robot controls course, I would complete it while still leading my crew; otherwise I would keep my current shifts and review our retirement figures with Mariam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We have several months saved and Mariam earns. Cuts to my cable crew shifts and paid evening class would change when I can afford to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the controls course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if we could afford it after the household bills, and I doubt we would choose that. My first ask is paid company training while the old work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No decision yet. I would work to our existing date if the shifts continue, and I would revisit it if an actual income cut changes the sums.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** cannot make an underground joint; any 2031 robot needs a human field trial.
I would ask the **union branch** to press for paid trials and named human sign-off.
think: The **2031 robot date** lands near the retirement date Mariam and I are considering.
Cuts to my **crew shifts** and paid class could force a later, not earlier, exit.
do: Join the **union branch** request for paid robot trials and human sign-off.
Complete a **paid controls course** if the company offers one while crew shifts continue.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible cut to both earnings streams near retirement.
S2.quote: Cuts to my cable crew shifts and paid evening class would change when I can afford to retire.
fieldNote: His moderate savings and Mariam’s wage give some **room to adjust**, not certainty.
Training depends on a **paid company place**; merely reviewing retirement figures does not imply an early exit.

steps.text: Join union request for paid robot trials and human sign-off
Complete paid cable-robot controls training if the company offers a place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives crews time to test cable robots in muddy pits, not only clean workshops. A robot in 2034 should have to pass the same safety checks as my apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may rewrite our permits, which I can check. If my health and the household numbers hold, I expect to be out of regular line work before robots arrive in 2034, though the class may still be mine to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the underground crew running next year and take the new starter into a real jointing pit each Friday. I would ask Mariam to review our savings and her work plans with me twice a year before we settle the retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm for my own job. I still worry that younger workers could be shown a screen before they are shown a cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave sooner because of 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our date depends on money and health, and I do not need to bring it forward just because the machine has a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new starter learn in the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How water creeps into a bad seal. The new starter has to clean the joint face and see a fault with their own eyes before relying on a readout.

say: I would demand **muddy-pit trials** before 2034 robots are accepted for cable joints.
I would argue that **new starters** still need hands-on fault practice.
think: I expect to leave regular field work before **2034** if health and household accounts hold.
The **2031 permit change** seems manageable because I already check AI job packs.
do: Keep leading the **underground crew** and teach the new starter in a jointing pit.
Review **retirement finances** with Mariam twice yearly before choosing a date.
feel: **Calm** about my own wage, with concern for apprentice training.
S3.quote: A robot in 2034 should have to pass the same safety checks as my apprentices.
fieldNote: He expects a conditional exit before the **robot phase**, without changing the retirement plan yet.
He uses the five-year runway for **site teaching** and household review, both already available to him.

steps.text: Keep leading cable joints and teach the new starter in real pits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my colleagues that a decade is enough to write proper rules with workers at the table. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 should not arrive at a cable pit without that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be close to seventy when thinking AI arrives, so I expect my climbing and digging days to be done. Our savings still need tending, but the timing does not threaten my present crew wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on with the crew this year and keep teaching the college class while it is offered. At our next union meeting I would propose a written standard for robot testing in flooded cable pits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself and rather determined for the younger hands. The long lead time is useful only if people do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should sign the proposed standard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A working cable jointer, the company safety lead and whoever maintains the machine. The worker must have a way to stop a trial when the pit is unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in a robot personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I work for an electricity company and do not own the crew equipment; buying one myself would make no sense.

say: I would propose **worker-written rules** before thinking AI and 2039 robots reshape cable work.
I would ask for **flooded-pit trials** with a crew member able to stop unsafe work.
think: I expect to have left **regular field work** before 2036 on our current timetable.
The long lead time protects my **present wage** but leaves younger crews needing a voice.
do: Keep **cable crew shifts** and the paid college class while both are offered.
Propose a **robot trial standard** at the next union meeting.
feel: **Calm** for my own household, determined about future crew safety.
S4.quote: The worker must have a way to stop a trial when the pit is unsafe.
fieldNote: His own likely exit precedes the **thinking date** without a promised pension or early retirement.
The union action is an actual **group meeting** with a specific proposed standard.

steps.text: Keep leading cable shifts and teaching the paid college class
Propose flooded cable pit robot trial rules at the next union meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a crew cut and a lost college class together could change what Mariam, my wife, and I can afford before I retire. Paid controls training and a real union role in field trials would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to stop a robot trial when water enters a cable pit. A shiny machine does not take responsibility for a worker in a flooded hole.

headlineQuote: A shiny machine does not take responsibility for a worker in a flooded hole.
portrait: **Colin**, 58, leads underground cable work with a technical diploma, typical trade pay and a few months of savings.
He uses **AI daily** for job packs and teaches a paid evening class alongside his electricity company work.
His **union focus** turns technology concerns into crew review, paid trials and a specific flooded-pit safety standard.
The **2028 case** worries him because field shifts and teaching pay might both change near retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could threaten crew and teaching income together before his planned exit.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **controls training** and a union voice in field trials would help him plan.
